title: Testing a pricer
objectives: Test a pricer against limits, put-call parity and known prices.

screens.title: Where the price goes
screens.prose: Here is the Black-Scholes call at $S = K = 100$, $r = 5\%$, $T = 1$, as volatility $\sigma$ changes. Drag the point towards the left edge. With no volatility at all, the share simply grows at the risk-free rate.
screens.question: As $\sigma \to 0$, what does the call's price approach, in £?

hints.text: Drag the point to $\sigma = 0.01$ and read the caption.
Without volatility the share ends at $100e^{0.05}$ for sure.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag the point to the far left and read the caption.

byKey.zero: An at-the-money call with no volatility is not worthless: the share drifts up at 5%, so it ends in the money for sure.
byKey.nodisc: £5.127 is the payoff in a year. Discount it to today: $100 - 100e^{-0.05}$.

explain.text: With $\sigma = 0$ the share ends at $100e^{0.05}$, so the call pays $100e^{0.05} - 100$ for sure, worth $100 - 100e^{-0.05} = 4.8771$ today. A known answer at an extreme like this is a **limit**, and it makes a test.

screens.title: Deep in and out of the money
screens.prose: Now $\sigma = 20\%$ again and the share price $S$ moves. The dashed line is $S - Ke^{-rT}$, a forward bought today. Drag the point to both ends.
screens.question: At $S = 200$, deep in the money, which value is the call closest to?

options.why: You used the payoff today. The strike is paid in a year, so it is discounted: the call is worth $S - Ke^{-rT}$.
The call never beats the share itself; you still pay the strike. It is worth about £95 less.
That is the other end: far out of the money, at $S = 40$, the call is worth almost nothing.

hints.text: Drag the point to $S = 200$ and compare it with the dashed line.
The dashed line is the forward.

feedback.correct: Deep in the money the call is a forward; deep out it is worth nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag to $S = 200$ and read the caption.

explain.text: At $S = 200$ the call is £104.8777, against $200 - 95.1229 = 104.8771$. At $S = 50$ it is £0.0024. Both limits are values a test can check without any formula of its own.

screens.title: Your first two tests
screens.prose: The hidden code gives you a small test kit: `TEST(name) { ... }` registers a test, and `CHECK_CLOSE(a, b, tol)` fails it when $|a - b| > \text{tol}$. Write a **put-call parity** test, $C - P = S - Ke^{-rT}$, and the $\sigma \to 0$ **limit test** for the call.
screens.question: Fill in both tests. Check also runs them against two planted bugs.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Test 1 runs your tests on correct pricers. Test 2 swaps in a put that forgets to discount the strike: your parity test must fail and the limit test pass. Test 3 does the same to the call: both must fail.

hints.text: Inside a test, compute both sides and compare them with `CHECK_CLOSE`.
Parity: `CHECK_CLOSE(bs_call(...) - bs_put(...), s - k * std::exp(-r * t), 1e-9);`

feedback.correct: Two tests, and both bite on real bugs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the PASS and FAIL lines under each test row.

byKey.test-2: With the put's discount missing, your parity test should fail. Does it compare $C - P$ with $S - Ke^{-rT}$, not with $S - K$?
byKey.test-3: With the call's discount missing, both tests should fail. Does each test call `bs_call` and check against a value it does not get from `bs_call`?

explain.text:
Parity links two pricers by a law that holds for any model without arbitrage, so it catches a bug in either. The limit pins the call to a value from first principles. Neither test copies the formula it tests.

```cpp
CHECK_CLOSE(c - p, s - k * std::exp(-r * t), 1e-9);
```

screens.title: The tree must converge
screens.prose: Level 2's tree tends to Black-Scholes as $n$ grows: at $n = 512$ it is 10.4467, within 0.004 of 10.4506. A **convergence test** checks that, with a tolerance tight enough to bite. Check plants two bugs: a tree that quietly stops at 64 steps, and one that drops the interest rate.
screens.question: Write the convergence test: `tree_call` at $n = 512$ within 0.01 of `bs_call`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Three hidden runs of your test: on the correct tree it passes; on a tree capped at 64 steps (10.4194) and on one with the rate dropped it must fail.

hints.text: Price both, then `CHECK_CLOSE` them.
Tolerance `0.01`: the capped tree is 0.031 away, the correct one 0.004.

feedback.correct: Tight enough to catch a tree 0.03 off, loose enough for the 0.004 the tree really has.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the PASS and FAIL lines under each row.

byKey.test-2: Your test passed a tree stuck at 64 steps, 0.031 away. Is the tolerance looser than 0.01, or is $n$ below 512?
byKey.test-1: Your test failed the correct tree. At $n = 512$ it is 0.004 from Black-Scholes, so 0.01 must pass.

explain.text: The tolerance comes from what we know: the tree's error at $n = 512$ is about 0.004, so 0.01 passes it with room. A tolerance of 0.05 would pass the capped tree too, and then the test could never fail on that bug.

screens.title: A test that agrees with itself
screens.question: Suppose `norm_cdf` has a bug. Does this test catch it?

options.text: No: `expected` uses the same `norm_cdf`, so both sides carry the bug and still agree
Yes: a tolerance of 1e-12 is strict enough to catch anything
options.why: A strict tolerance only helps if the two sides are computed differently. Here both share the faulty function, so they match to every digit.

options.text: Yes: it works out $d_1$ and $d_2$ by hand
options.why: Writing $d_1$ out again is not independent: the result still goes through the same `norm_cdf` as the pricer.

options.text: No, because 1e-12 is too loose
options.why: The tolerance is fine. The flaw is that the expected value repeats the code under test.

hints.text: Which functions does `expected` call?
If `norm_cdf` returned the wrong number, what would happen to both sides?

feedback.correct: A test that recomputes the formula is circular.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow a wrong `norm_cdf` through both sides.

byKey.tight: You trusted the tolerance, but both sides use the same `norm_cdf`. A wrong value on one side is the same wrong value on the other.

explain.text: The expected value repeats the pricer's own steps, so any bug in them cancels. Check against something independent: a published value (10.4506), a limit, parity, or a different method such as the tree. Here `CHECK_CLOSE(bs_call(...), 10.4506, 1e-4)` would do.

screens.title: Catch the planted bug
screens.prose: Somebody changed one character in `bs_put`: it now uses $N(d_2)$ where it needs $N(-d_2)$. Write exactly one test that fails on that version and passes on the correct one. The correct put at the standard inputs is £5.5735.
screens.question: Write one `TEST` that catches the changed `bs_put`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Three hidden runs: the planted $N(d_2)$ bug must make your test fail, the correct put must make it pass, and a second bug (the strike not discounted, 7.7213) must also fail it.

hints.text: What do you know about the put that does not come from `bs_put` itself?
A known value (5.5735), or parity with `bs_call`.

feedback.correct: Your test fails on the bug and passes on the fix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read which run went the wrong way.

byKey.test-1: Your test passed the bugged put. A check such as `bs_put(...) > 0` holds for both: compare with an independent value.
byKey.test-2: Your test failed the correct put. Is the tolerance at least 1e-4 against the rounded 5.5735?

explain.text: A good test is one a plausible bug cannot pass. The known value 5.5735 or put-call parity both work; `bs_put(...) > 0` does not, because 16.9155 is positive too. Planting a bug on purpose is how you test your tests.

screens.title: A Greek by bumping
screens.prose:
Delta is $\partial C/\partial S$, and the pricer has a closed form, `bs_delta_call`, which is $N(d_1)$. Check it against the **central difference**

$$\Delta \approx \frac{C(S + h) - C(S - h)}{2h},$$

whose error shrinks like $h^2$. With $h = 0.01$ it is about $10^{-8}$ here, so a tolerance of $10^{-5}$ has room.
screens.question: Write the finite-difference delta test with $h = 0.01$ and tolerance 1e-5.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Three hidden runs: the correct delta passes; a delta of $N(d_2)$ (0.5596) and one discounted by $e^{-rT}$ (0.6058) must each fail.

hints.text: Price the call at $S + h$ and $S - h$.
`double fd = (up - down) / (2 * h);`
`CHECK_CLOSE(bs_delta_call(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1), fd, 1e-5);`

feedback.correct: The closed form and the bump agree to about 1e-8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read which run went the wrong way.

byKey.test-1: Your test failed the correct delta. Divide by `2 * h`, and bump `s`, not `k`.
byKey.test-3: Your test passed a delta 0.03 off. Is the tolerance 1e-5?

explain.text: The bump uses only `bs_call`, so it is independent of `bs_delta_call`. Its error is about $h^2/6$ times the third derivative, here $9 \times 10^{-9}$. Too small an $h$ fails differently: at $h = 10^{-12}$ rounding in the subtraction swamps the answer.

screens.title: A test file for a pricer
screens.question: A **property test** loops over 1,000 seeded random inputs and checks the call rises with $\sigma$. It passes. What does that show?

options.text: The property holds on those 1,000 inputs, and the run repeats exactly; it is not a proof for every input
The property holds for every possible input
options.why: 1,000 points are a sample. A bug confined to, say, tiny $T$ could fall between them.

options.text: Nothing, because random inputs make the test flaky
options.why: The seed fixes the inputs, so every run checks the same 1,000 cases.

options.text: That the price is correct
options.why: A price can rise with $\sigma$ and still be wrong. Monotonicity is one property among several.

hints.text: What does the fixed seed guarantee, and what can 1,000 points not guarantee?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a fixed seed fixes.

explain.text: A seeded loop is a hand-made property test: the same inputs every run, so a failure can be replayed, but only those inputs are checked. Combine it with limits, parity, known values and a Greek, as in the tree.

screens.title: C++ against Python
screens.prose: The exit task: your C++ tree must match the Python tree of the trees course. A regression test prices 100 seeded random inputs in both and compares them with `==`. It passed on the debug build. CTest now runs it on the release build, `-O2 -march=native`.

lines: 67% tests passed, 1 tests failed out of 3
params.title: Desk terminal

screens.question: Both trees are correct. What should the comparison use?

options.text: A relative tolerance of about 1e-9
Keep `==`: the release build has a bug in its last digit
options.why: `-march=native` lets the compiler fuse a multiply and an add into one rounding. Both prices are correct; they differ by one part in $10^{15}$.

options.text: An absolute tolerance of 0.01
options.why: Too loose: a tree capped at 64 steps is only 0.03 off, and a bug of 0.005 would pass.

options.text: An absolute tolerance of 1e-17
options.why: That is below the spacing of doubles near 10, about 1.8e-15, so it is `==` in disguise.

hints.text: How far apart are the two prices?
Compare the two numbers on line 6.
Same algorithm, different rounding: allow a few parts in a billion.

feedback.correct: Same algorithm, so they should agree to about nine significant figures, not every bit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at how far apart the two prices are.

explain.text: The prices differ by $1.1 \times 10^{-15}$ relative: a fused multiply-add rounds once where Python rounds twice. A relative 1e-9 accepts that and still catches any real bug. With that test passing on 100 inputs, and l9's timings, the exit task is done: the C++ pricer, tested and timed against Python.

ideas: Test a pricer against things it does not compute itself: limits, parity, published values, another method, and finite differences for Greeks.
Choose each tolerance from the known error: tight enough that a plausible bug fails, loose enough for rounding. Never `==` on doubles.
Test your tests: plant a bug and watch the test fail. Seeded property loops are repeatable but not exhaustive.
summary.trap: A test that recomputes the formula under test agrees with itself and catches nothing.

quiz.prose: You want a test that `bs_call` with $\sigma < 0$ throws `std::invalid_argument`.
quiz.question: Where can that test run?

options.text: On a desk build, as `REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(..., std::invalid_argument)`; this app cannot catch exceptions
Here, with `try` and `catch` inside a `TEST`
options.why: This app's runtime has no unwinder: a `throw` always ends the program, so `catch` never runs.

options.text: Nowhere: C++ cannot test for exceptions
options.why: Catch2's `REQUIRE_THROWS` and GoogleTest's `EXPECT_THROW` do exactly that on a normal build.

options.text: Here, by asserting that the price is NaN
options.why: A throw does not return a NaN; it never returns at all.

feedback.correct: Exception tests belong on a full desk build.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what this app does with a `throw`.

explain.text: Catch2's `REQUIRE_THROWS_AS` catches the exception and passes. In this app a throw ends the whole program, so the test file would stop there; a code widget can only check that the program stops, with a `raises` case.
